It was not haunted.

This disappointed Nell, who had brought a flashlight, a kitchen knife, and three questions for her dead mother.

Instead of ghosts, she found dust, a collapsed staircase, and a small brass bell on the kitchen table. Beside it lay a card.

**Ring only if you have lost something.**

Nell set down the knife.

She rang.

Somewhere beneath the floor, machinery shuddered awake. A narrow door opened where a cupboard had been.

Behind it stood a man wearing a waistcoat made entirely of pockets.

“You’re late,” he said.

“For what?”

He checked a watch without hands. “Hard to say. Come in.”

The stairs behind him descended much farther than the house should have allowed. At the bottom, shelves stretched into a warm, golden distance. They held single gloves, wedding rings, umbrellas, teeth. Bottles contained laughter. A blue kite fluttered beneath a glass dome.

“Lost property,” the man explained.

“All of it?”

“Everything that hasn’t been destroyed. Things people gave up looking for. Things they never noticed were missing.”

Nell stopped beside a jar marked **COURAGE, AGE SEVEN**.

“Whose?”

“Yours.”

Inside, something small and yellow battered against the glass.

She moved on.

At a desk, the man opened an enormous ledger.

“What have you lost?”

“My mother.”

His expression changed.

“People don’t come here.”

“But you said—”

“Lost,” he said gently. “Not gone.”

Nell stared at the ledger until its neat columns blurred.

The man waited. Above them, pipes ticked in the silence.

Then Nell said, “I can’t remember her voice.”

He turned a page.

“She used to say something when she tucked me in. I remember that she said it. I remember laughing. But I can’t hear it anymore.”

The man ran one finger down a column.

“Ah.”

He fetched a little wooden box from a shelf behind his desk. There was a pale crescent on its lid, like the moon Nell’s mother used to draw on her lunch bags.

“What does it cost?” Nell asked.

“One thing you’ve kept that you no longer need.”

She searched her pockets. A bus ticket. A hair elastic. Forty-seven pence.

“Not those.”

Nell looked at him.

He waited again.

At last she said, “I was angry with her.”

The man sat down.

“The morning of the accident. She wouldn’t let me go to a friend’s house, and I told her I wished she’d leave me alone.” Nell pressed her thumbnail into her palm. “I didn’t say goodbye when she went to work.”

From somewhere in the shelves came the faint sound of a dog barking, delighted to have been found.

“If I give that away,” Nell asked, “will I forget?”

“No.”

“Then what changes?”

“You’ll still wish you’d said goodbye. But you won’t have to keep punishing yourself for being twelve.”

Nell stood very still.

Then she opened her hand.

A small grey stone lay in her palm. She had never seen it before, though its weight was horribly familiar.

She placed it on the desk.

The man gave her the box.

Inside was nothing she could see.

But when she lifted the lid, her mother said, clear and close, “Goodnight, pickle. Try not to turn into a frog.”

Nell laughed.

It hurt. Then it didn’t.

When she finally climbed back into the kitchen, dawn was brightening the broken windows. She tucked the box carefully into her coat.

At the front door, she paused.

“Does anyone ever come back?”

“All the time,” the man said.

Nell thought of the yellow thing beating its wings inside the jar.

“Could you keep my courage somewhere easy to reach?”

“For next time?”

She nodded.

The man smiled and slipped a hand into one of his many pockets.

“No need,” he said. “It’s been following you upstairs.”"}
